A commenter who has built robots full time for 7 years said they struggled to tell which real-world use cases Viam's system design is based on, or which alternative architectures it improves on. They called the website's use-case section 'too meta to be useful' and said industrial users prefer 'reliable', 'well understood', or 'cheap' over 'modern'.

One user's reading of the platform: the robot hardware must provide a TCP stack, and firmware must be written against the Viam SDK, which requires a high-level OS such as Linux on the robot. They likened Viam to 'LabView/Simulink or ROS as-a-web-service'.
A commenter flagged as a drawback that the firmware running on the robot needs internet access to work with the platform.

A user liked the idea of a managed cloud but was unsure how much of Viam is actually open source. They said they would hesitate to rely on it in production, since cloud providers that go out of business can brick many IoT devices, and asked whether the server could be self-hosted.
